About this document

This document provides the teaching content for Physics Years 12–13 of the
New Zealand Curriculum. Equivalent for Te Marautanga o Aotearoa is being
published separately.

Progress and assessment information for Physics Years 12–13 is still in development.
Once that is completed, Physics Years 12–13 is proposed to be made by the Minister
of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under section 90(1)(a) of the
Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Physics Years 12–13 will be required to start using it in Year 12 from
1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January 2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

Purpose statement
                                                                                         Mā te whakaaro nui e hanga te whare;   By great thought the house is built;
                                                                                         mā te mātauranga e whakaū.             by knowledge it is made firm.




 Students are taught about key areas of physics, including mechanics, waves,
 electromagnetism, and modern physics including quantum phenomena. Students
 are taught how to examine and use experimental techniques, mathematical
 modelling, and the fundamental concepts of physics to explain the natural world.

Through the study of Physics, students are taught to apply and extend knowledge of
matter, energy, motion, forces, fields, waves, and interactions across a wide range of
scales. They investigate how physical systems behave and interact, and how
mathematical relationships, models, and evidence are used to explain observations
and make predictions. Students use measurements, graphical representations,
experiments, and mathematical analysis to investigate physical phenomena and
communicate scientific understanding.
Physics provides students with the knowledge and practices to analyse systems,
evaluate evidence, test predictions, and understand the underlying principles
governing the natural world. Students develop the ability to apply scientific and
mathematical reasoning to solve problems, interpret experimental data, and evaluate
explanations and models. They are taught how physical principles are applied in
technologies that shape society and influence future innovation.
As students progress through Years 12–13 Physics, they are supported to develop
their understanding of disciplinary concepts, mathematical relationships, scientific
models, experimental methods, and technical terminology. This enables students to
communicate scientific reasoning using accurate measurements, calculations,
graphical analysis, and evidence-based explanations.

 Physics provides a foundation for success across a range of subjects including
 Mathematics, Chemistry, Earth and Space Science, Engineering, Electronics, and
 Computer Science. The teaching of Physics supports student pathways across
 fields such as engineering, medicine, aviation, architecture, astronomy, data
 science, energy systems, technology, and scientific research.

Science is a collaborative human activity that develops knowledge of the natural
world. This knowledge enables scientists to create technologies, inventions, and
innovations that benefit society and help solve problems. Because scientific
knowledge can have both positive and negative impacts, it must be applied
responsibly. In New Zealand, science is closely connected to kaitiakitanga,
recognising responsibilities of guardianship and care for the natural world. Scientists
communicate their ideas, evidence, and findings so they can be evaluated,
challenged, and used to inform decisions and actions.
Investigating in science
Scientists develop meaningful questions and use investigations to explain
phenomena. They gather or select evidence, collect primary data or source
secondary data, analyse data, identify patterns and relationships, evaluate evidence,
consider alternative explanations, and distinguish between strong and weak support
for claims. Scientists test theories by attempting to falsify them rather than prove
them.
At Years 12 and 13, students continue to investigate scientific questions, gather and
analyse evidence, and use this evidence to explain scientific phenomena and develop
their understanding of Physics.
Opportunities should be provided each year for students to undertake both practical
and secondary-source investigations, working independently and collaboratively.
Contexts and investigations may be selected or developed to reflect the needs and
interests of students, their community, and the local environment.
Delivery of the Year 12 and 13 Physics programme must align with Safety and
Science guidance.
Further guidance on programme design, investigation opportunities, and resource
selection is available in the Physics Curriculum Support Document.

                                  Nucleon number and charge are conserved in nuclear

                                   and two neutrons that has been ejected from an unstable
                                   nucleus.
                                  A beta particle is a fast-moving positron ( 01𝛽𝛽) or electron
                                   ( −10𝛽𝛽) that has been ejected from an unstable nucleus.
                                  A gamma ray ( 00𝛾𝛾) is a high-energy wave that has been

                                   different penetrating powers, interactions with magnetic
                                   fields, and ionising effects based on their mass, charge,
                                   and energy.

                                   with electrons, annihilating each other and releasing
                                   energy.
                                  A level of background radiation exists everywhere. This
                                   comes from sources such as cosmic rays and naturally
                                   occurring radioisotopes.
                                  Radioactive decay is random and spontaneous. The
                                   number of undecayed nuclei in a sample of a radioisotope
                                   decreases according to a predictable exponential decay
                                   pattern.

                                   how long it takes for half the nuclei of the radioisotope to
                                   decay.
